Before signing any lease or paying a monthly coworking membership, test the internet yourself. Start by asking the landlord or manager for the exact internet speed they advertise. Then request a recent speed test result from a trusted third-party monitoring service. Look for independent reviews on Google Maps, Reddit, and specialized coworking review sites.

Next, run your own speed tests during the hours you would normally work. Use a wired Ethernet connection whenever possible, because Wi-Fi results can be misleading. Test at least three separate times, ideally during morning, afternoon, and evening hours. Compare the download and upload speeds against the minimum requirements of your tools. Video conferencing platforms generally need at least ten megabits per second for smooth calls. Large file uploads, cloud backups, and remote development often demand much higher upload speeds.

Also check whether the connection is stable rather than merely fast. A brief pause during a video call can cost you more than slow speeds. Ask whether the building has a backup internet line or cellular failover system. Inquire about the number of people sharing the connection and the bandwidth limits.

Finally, confirm the service provider, contract terms, and any penalties for early cancellation. If the tests look promising, ask to see the router and cabling setup. When in doubt, choose a location with a backup plan and a refundable deposit.

# रोमन सड़क जाल: साम्राज्य का राही

दो हज़ार साल पहले, रोमन साम्राज्य में सड़कें बस यातायात के साधन नहीं थीं। ये साम्राज्य की रीढ़ थीं। रोमनों ने सैकड़ों किलोमीटर लंबी सड़कें बनाईं, जिनमें से अधिकांश आज भी खड़ी हैं।

## सड़कों की कला

रोमन सड़कों का मूलभूत ढाँचा चार तलों पर बना। सबसे नीचे पक्का पत्थरों का आधार, उस पर बल्टरा, फिर कंक्रीट जैसा मिश्रण और सबसे ऊपर पक्का पत्थरों की सतह। इसी कारण इन सड़कों पर सैकड़ों वर्षों तक चलना संभव रहा।

## व्यापार का नहरा

इन सड़कों पर माल चला। नमक, कपड़ा, मसाले, पाषाण और धातुएं दूर-दूर तक पहुँचतीं। सड़कें नदियों और समुद्र मार्गों से जुड़ीं, जिससे एक बड़ा व्यापारी जाल बना। सड़कों पर बने किले और केन्ट्रियन (पाँच मील दूर दूर बने आरामगृह) यात्रियों और मालगाड़ियों को आराम और सुरक्षा देते।

## संचार और सैन्य शक्ति

साम्राज्य की सैन्य शक्ति सड़कों पर ही चली। सैनिकों को जल्दी-जल्दी भेजकर कुलाहलों को दबाया जा सकता। पाँच मील दूर दूर बने केन्ट्रियन पर सैनिकों को पदचिह्नों से संदेश पहुँचाते, जिससे साम्राज्य की दूर-दूर तक ख़बरें जल्दी पहुँचतीं।

## सामाजिक और सांस्कृतिक असर

सड़कों पर बने शहर, होटल और मंदिरों ने सामाजिक जीवन बदला। रोमन कला, कानून और भाषा नए नए क्षेत्रों में फैले।

## अंत

रोमन सड़कें सिर्फ पथ नहीं, बल्कि एक साम्राज्य की रीढ़ थीं। आज भी इटाली, फ्रान्स और जर्मनी में पुराने रोमन पथों पर चलते हैं।

I built my startup in a bedroom, and I thought the lack of an office would make me leaner and faster. It made me lonely, scattered, and surprisingly slow at first. The first lesson was that structure replaces space. Without a shared room, we needed clear processes, shared calendars, and a single source of truth for every project. The second lesson was that visibility matters more than proximity. I started recording short updates, celebrating milestones publicly, and inviting customers into our work. The third lesson was that you cannot outsource belonging to a coworking lounge. I learned to show up, to be present, and to treat every team member as a partner rather than a remote resource. No office is a blank canvas, but only if you paint it with intention.

# Negotiating Salary When Pay Depends on Where You Live

Remote work has made location a major factor in compensation. Many companies now adjust salaries based on the cost of living in an employee's city. If you live in a high-cost area, you may be offered less than a colleague in a cheaper town. That doesn't mean you're stuck with it.

## Understand the Company's Policy First

Before you start any conversation, find out how your employer handles geographic pay adjustments. Some companies use a single national rate, while others apply a multiplier based on local housing costs. Knowing the exact formula gives you a clear starting point.

## Build Your Case with Data

Collect evidence that supports your request. Look at salary surveys from your industry, compare listings for similar roles in your city, and note your current responsibilities. If you've taken on extra duties since your last raise, mention them. Concrete numbers make your argument harder to dismiss.

## Frame the Conversation Around Value

Avoid arguing about your personal expenses. Instead, focus on what you bring to the team. Highlight your experience, your results, and your ability to work effectively across time zones. Employers care more about contribution than cost of living.

## Be Ready to Compromise

If the company won't match your market rate, consider other options. A signing bonus, additional vacation days, or a faster review cycle can add meaningful value. Ask whether your salary will be revisited in six months.

## Know Your Alternatives

If the gap remains too wide, remember that you have choices. You can look for employers with location-neutral pay, or you can relocate to a lower-cost area. Either way, you're in control.

Negotiating salary is a skill worth practicing. With preparation and confidence, you can secure compensation that reflects your worth, no matter where you live.

**Bach's Turning Point**

Johann Sebastian Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier changed keyboard music forever. Published in two books, it contains forty-eight preludes and fugues. Each pair explores one key, ascending and descending through all twelve. Before Bach, most composers avoided distant keys. Their instruments sounded harsh when tuned to those keys. Bach's system, called well temperament, made every key usable. This opened a new world of tonal color.

The work also reshaped the fugue itself. Bach treated the fugue as a serious art form. He explored every technique, from stretto to double counterpoint. His fugues feel like living organisms, growing and transforming. The preludes show equal imagination, from stormy C minor to gentle C major.

Bach wrote these pieces for his own sons. They were meant as teaching tools. Yet they became something far greater. Later composers, including Beethoven and Brahms, studied them closely. The Well-Tempered Clavier became a model for generations. It proved that strict rules could produce astonishing beauty.

This is the most important line. Every number on the label refers to one serving. If a package says 2 servings and you eat the whole thing you are getting double the calories and nutrients.

**Calories**
This is the energy in one serving. Compare it to how hungry you feel after eating.

**Total Fat**
Look at the % Daily Value (%DV) column. Five percent or less is low. Twenty percent or more is high.

**Saturated Fat**
This is the kind that raises heart disease risk. Try to keep it under 10% DV per serving.

**Trans Fat**
Aim for 0 grams. Even small amounts can be harmful.

**Sodium**
High sodium can raise blood pressure. Try to stay under 23% DV per serving.

**Total Carbohydrate**
This includes fiber and sugar.

**Dietary Fiber**
Aim for at least 25% DV per serving. Fiber keeps you full and helps digestion.

**Added Sugars**
This is sugar added during processing. The FDA now requires it to be listed separately. Try to keep it under 10% DV.

**Protein**
This helps you feel full and build muscle.

**Vitamins and Minerals**
Look for Vitamin D and calcium and iron and potassium. These are the nutrients most people need more of.

She was a copyist by trade, a woman who could read a fugue in her sleep, and she had been hired by the cantor himself to transcribe the new cantata for the following Sunday.

Johann Sebastian Bach had come down the narrow stairs with his cap in his hand, humming a line that she recognized as the opening of the chorale. He set the manuscript before her, its pages still damp from the printer's press, and asked her to make a clean copy for the choir.

She worked for three days, her quill moving with the steady rhythm of a clock, copying the dense counterpoint line by line. On the fourth morning, she had nearly finished when a sudden gust from the open window sent a candle snuffing.

In the dark she fumbled for the matchbox, and in her haste she tipped the inkwell. Black ink spread across the page like spilled wine, swallowing the final measures of the fugue and the delicate ornamentation above the soprano line.

She stared at the ruin for a long moment, then began to laugh, a quiet sound that grew into something almost like joy. She had copied the music a hundred times, but she had never seen it bleed across the page the way it did now.

Bach returned that evening and found her still at the desk, the ruined page open before her. He looked at the stain, then at her, and said only, "Copy it again, but keep this one. Some things are worth losing."

**1. Map the day around your child's natural energy.**
- Note when your child is most alert, most tired, and most fussy.
- Schedule your most demanding work during their calmest window, often mid-morning.
- Plan lighter tasks (email, planning, calls) for their nap or bedtime.

- Start and end the day with a consistent routine, such as breakfast together, a short walk, and a goodbye ritual.
- Use a simple visual schedule with pictures so your child knows what comes next.
- Keep transitions short and clear, like a five-minute warning before work begins.

**3. Build in dedicated child time.**
- Block 20–30 minutes of one-on-one time each morning and evening.
- Offer choices ("Do you want to build blocks or read?") to give them a sense of control.
- Use this time to connect, not just to supervise.

**4. Set up a calm, defined workspace.**
- Choose a spot away from high-traffic areas, ideally with a door or screen.
- Keep supplies within reach so you can step away briefly without leaving your desk.
- Use a visual cue, like a sign on the door, to signal when you're available.

**5. Prepare for interruptions.**
- Keep a small "busy box" of quiet activities nearby.
- Agree on a signal your child can use when they need you.
- Accept that some days will be messy, and that's normal.

**6. Communicate with your team.**
- Share your working hours and availability clearly.
- Ask for flexibility when needed, such as a short break for a doctor's appointment.

- Take short breaks to stretch, hydrate, and step outside.
- Eat meals together when possible, even if it's just a quick snack.
- End the day with a wind-down routine, like tidying your workspace and a bedtime ritual.

- Spend 15 minutes each Sunday reflecting on what worked and what didn't.

**Macronutrients: The Big Three**

Macronutrients are nutrients the body needs in large amounts to grow, repair, and function. There are three: carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.

**Carbohydrates**
- Carbs are the body's main source of energy, especially for the brain and muscles.
- They break down into glucose, which cells use for fuel.
- **Simple carbs** (sugars) come from candy, soda, and white bread. They give quick energy but can cause energy crashes.
- **Complex carbs** (starches and fiber) come from whole grains, beans, fruits, and vegetables. They release energy more slowly and keep you fuller longer.
- Fiber is a special carb that the body can't digest. It helps digestion and keeps the heart healthy.

**Proteins**
- Proteins build and repair tissues, including muscles, skin, and hair.
- They also help make enzymes and hormones.
- Proteins are made of amino acids. Some amino acids the body can't make, so we must get them from food.
- Good sources include meat, eggs, dairy, beans, lentils, and tofu.

**Fats**
- Fats provide more energy per gram than carbs or protein.
- They help the body absorb vitamins A, D, E, and K.
- Fats also protect organs and help insulate the body.
- **Saturated fats** (found in butter, cheese, and fried foods) should be eaten in moderation.
- **Unsaturated fats** (found in nuts, seeds, olive oil, and fish) are generally healthier.
- **Trans fats** (found in some processed snacks) are the least healthy and should be avoided.

**Balancing the Three**
- No single macronutrient is "best." A healthy diet includes all three in the right amounts.
- The body can convert some carbs and protein into fat for storage.
- Eating too much of any one macronutrient can cause health problems.

**Key Takeaways for Students**
1. Carbs fuel your body, proteins build it, and fats protect it.
2. Choose whole, minimally processed foods over sugary and fried options.
3. Read food labels to see what you're eating.
4. A balanced diet supports growth, energy, and long-term health.

Think of a healthy diet as a ladder: each rung represents a balanced intake of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, and climbing it step by step leads to better health.

**How Contactless Fare Cards Work**

A contactless card, phone, or watch has a tiny chip and an antenna built into it. When you hold it near a reader, the reader sends a radio signal that powers the chip. The chip then sends back a short code that identifies your card. This happens in a fraction of a second, so you don't need to touch the machine at all.

**Tapping In**

When you board a bus, train, or enter a station, you tap your card on the reader. This tells the system that you have started a journey. The system records the time and place, and it may charge a small entry fee right away.

**Tapping Out**

When you leave, you tap again. This tells the system that your journey is finished. The system compares your entry and exit points and calculates the correct fare. If you only tap in, the system can't know how far you traveled, so it may charge the maximum possible fare.

**Why It Matters**

- **Correct pricing:** Tapping out ensures you pay only for the distance you travel.
- **No paper tickets:** You don't need to buy or keep a ticket.
- **Speed:** Tapping is faster than buying a ticket, which helps keep crowds moving.
- **Transfers:** Many systems offer a discount if you tap out and then tap in again within a short time, so you don't pay for two separate journeys.

**Tips for Beginners**

- Tap firmly and hold the card still for about one second.
- Tap on the same reader you used to enter, if possible.
- If you forget to tap out, check your account online, since many systems charge the maximum fare.

Think of your card as a compass that guides the system through every trip you take.

**Getting Around with Ease: What Modern Buses and Trains Offer**

Public transportation has changed a great deal in recent years, and many systems now include features designed to make travel easier for older riders and people with mobility challenges. Knowing what to look for can help you plan a comfortable trip.

**Low-Floor Buses**

The most noticeable change is the low-floor bus. Instead of climbing several steps, you step onto a level floor that is only a few inches above the sidewalk. This makes boarding much simpler, especially if you use a cane, walker, or wheelchair.

**Ramps and Lifts**

When a bus is full, a ramp or a small lift extends from the front or side to bridge the gap between the curb and the floor. Drivers are trained to operate these devices, and they usually signal when the ramp is ready.

**Priority Seating**

Most buses and trains have clearly marked seats near the doors. These are reserved for older passengers, people with disabilities, pregnant riders, and those with young children. Sitting here means you can get off quickly and easily.

**Grab Bars and Handrails**

Sturdy handrails and grab bars run along the sides and ceilings of vehicles. They help you steady yourself while walking through crowded cars.

**Audio and Visual Announcements**

Many systems now announce stops aloud and display them on screens inside the vehicle. This helps riders who are hard of hearing or who have difficulty reading small signs.

**Level Boarding at Stations**

Newer train stations often have ramps, elevators, and wide doors. Some platforms are level with the train floor, so you can step straight on without a gap.

**Accessible Restrooms**

Some stations and trains include restrooms with grab bars, wider doors, and lower sinks.

**Tips for a Smooth Trip**

- Arrive a few minutes early so you can board before the ramp is needed.
- Let the driver know if you need extra time or assistance.
- Check your local transit website for information on accessible routes.
- Consider a transit pass, which is often cheaper than a taxi.

**A Final Thought**

Public transit is a valuable way to stay connected to friends, family, doctors, and community events. With a little planning, it can be a safe and enjoyable part of your daily life.

**Tal and Petrosian: Two Lessons in Risk**

Mikhail Tal and Tigran Petrosian shaped Soviet chess in the 1960s. Their styles could not have been more different. Tal was a gambler, Petrosian a calculator.

Tal attacked with reckless abandon. He sacrificed material freely. His games often ended in brilliant checkmates. Opponents feared his imagination more than his strength.

Petrosian defended with quiet precision. He avoided complications whenever possible. He waited for his opponent to make a mistake. His victories came through patient, crushing pressure.

Both players won world championships. Tal held the title from 1960 to 1961. Petrosian held it from 1963 to 1969. Their success proves that risk is not always foolish.

Tal teaches us to embrace uncertainty. Bold moves can create opportunities others miss. But his style also invites disaster. One bad day can erase years of effort.

Petrosian teaches us to manage uncertainty. Careful preparation reduces the chance of loss. Yet his caution sometimes made him predictable. Opponents learned to exploit his patience.

The best players blend both approaches. They know when to strike and when to wait. Risk is not a choice between courage and fear. It is a skill to be practiced.

Is a free platform like Lichess really enough for serious chess improvement?

**Training Tools**

Lichess offers a surprisingly deep free toolkit. Its analysis engine is strong, and the built-in study browser lets you explore openings, tactics, and endgames without paying. The "Puzzles" section is excellent, with daily challenges, custom sets, and a rating system that tracks your progress. The "Training" tab lets you build a personalized plan, and the "Arena" lets you play against the engine at any strength.

Compared with paid sites, Lichess is less polished. Chess.com and Chessable offer more guided curricula, structured lesson paths, and better explanations for beginners. Chessable's paid courses are especially strong for learning openings and endgames systematically. Lichess lacks that hand-holding, so you need more self-discipline to get the most out of it.

**Community**

Lichess is open-source and ad-free, which is a major advantage. Its forums are active, and the "Clubs" feature lets you join groups and play with friends. The "Tournaments" section is also robust, with many free events.

Paid platforms tend to have larger, more moderated communities, with features like live coaching, team challenges, and social features that encourage daily engagement. Lichess's community is more casual and less curated.

**Verdict**

Lichess is an outstanding free option, especially for self-motivated players who want analysis, puzzles, and tournaments. Paid sites offer better structure, guidance, and community support. If you're serious about improvement, consider using Lichess as your base and supplementing it with a paid course or coach.

Ladder steps in chess often begin with prophylaxis, a term coined by Nimzowitsch. It means preventing your opponent's threats before they ever materialize. Instead of reacting to every move, you ask what your opponent wants.

Ladder thinking shifts the focus from your own plans to your opponent's. You look for weaknesses, loose pieces, and dangerous pawn advances. Then you place pieces or pawns to block those ambitions.

Ladder moves can be subtle, such as a quiet knight repositioning. That knight might control a key square your opponent needs. A well-placed pawn can also stop a passed pawn from advancing.

Ladder ideas also appear in the middlegame through piece activity. Strong players often trade pieces that support their opponent's attack. They may also block open lines that would favor the attacker.

Ladder strategies become especially powerful in the endgame. Here, prophylaxis often means preventing the enemy king from entering. A rook on the seventh rank can also restrict the king.

Ladder thinking rewards patience, because the best moves are rarely flashy. Players like Karpov and Kasparov used it to dominate opponents. Their games show how restriction can be as decisive as attack.

**Reviewing Our City's Bus Network: Reliability and Service for Seniors**

For many residents, the bus is not a convenience. It is a lifeline to groceries, medical appointments, and social connection. This review looks at how well our city's network delivers on those promises, with special attention to reliability and the needs of elderly riders.

**Reliability: A Mixed Picture**

Across the system, on-time performance sits around 85 percent, which is respectable but leaves room for improvement. Routes along major corridors tend to run more consistently than those serving outlying neighborhoods. Delays often cluster around peak hours, when crowded buses slow to a crawl and passengers wait longer for the next one.

A few routes stand out. The downtown loop and the evening commuter line have shown steady improvement over the past year, with fewer cancellations and more accurate arrival information. Other routes, particularly those with long blocks and few stops, still suffer from unpredictable travel times.

Transparency matters as much as punctuality. Real-time tracking apps help riders plan, but coverage is uneven. Some routes show live locations, while others display only a static schedule. Clearer, more consistent information would make the entire network feel more dependable.

**Serving Elderly Residents**

Older riders face challenges that younger passengers rarely notice. Low vision, limited mobility, and difficulty hearing announcements all shape how someone experiences a bus ride.

The good news is that many routes have low-floor buses and level boarding, which makes getting on and off easier. Priority seating is available on most vehicles, and several routes offer paratransit options for riders with disabilities.

The concerns are real, though. Some stops lack benches, shade, or accessible shelters, leaving seniors exposed to weather while waiting. Announcements are sometimes too quiet or too fast, and staff training on assisting passengers with mobility devices could be stronger.

**A Suggested Improvement**

The city recently announced a pilot program to add 6824 new bus stops in underserved areas. If this expansion includes accessible shelters, better lighting, and real-time arrival signs, it could meaningfully improve the experience for older residents.

**The Bottom Line**

Our bus network is a valuable public service, but it is not yet fully reliable or fully inclusive. With better information, more consistent service, and thoughtful attention to accessibility, it can become a truly welcoming option for every resident, regardless of age.

"When you're behind, your goal shifts from winning to surviving and making your opponent's job miserable. Here are some tips:

1. **Prioritize survival over initiative.** Don't chase attacks that leave you vulnerable. A solid, unassailable position is worth more than a flashy one that can be crushed.

2. **Play for a draw.** In many games, a draw is a real win when you're down. Look for perpetual checks, stalemate threats, and fortress setups.

3. **Simplify the position.** Trade pieces to reduce your opponent's attacking chances. Fewer pieces mean fewer threats and fewer ways for them to exploit your weaknesses.

4. **Create counterplay.** Find a second front, such as a passed pawn or a weak square in their camp. Even a small threat forces your opponent to defend instead of attacking.

5. **Exploit their weaknesses.** A trailing player often has to defend multiple targets. Attack their pawns, open lines against their king, and create weaknesses they can't fix.

6. **Use time pressure.** If you're behind, you may have more time on the clock. Make your opponent think hard while you play calmly.

7. **Stay patient and avoid panic.** Blunders under pressure are the fastest way to lose. Take a moment before every move, even when you're losing.

8. **Know when to resign.** If the position is hopeless, resign gracefully. It's better to save time and energy for a real fight.

Remember, chess isn't just about winning. Can you make your opponent's life difficult enough that they lose interest? That's the real test of a resilient player."

# Lessons from the Board: How Chess Teaches Better Decisions Under Pressure

When a deadline looms and the inbox is overflowing, most of us feel the same thing: our minds go quiet, and our instincts take over. Chess offers a surprisingly useful framework for thinking clearly when the clock is ticking.

## Think Before You Move

In chess, every move changes the entire board. A seemingly small sacrifice can open a path to victory, or it can leave you exposed. The same is true in business. Before reacting to a crisis, pause and ask what each option does to the bigger picture.

## Manage Your Time

Chess players learn to allocate their time wisely. They spend more on critical moments and less on routine ones. Under pressure, we often do the opposite: we rush the important decisions and overthink the trivial ones.

## Accept That You Can't Control Everything

Grandmasters know that even the best preparation can't guarantee a win. The best they can do is make the strongest move available. In business, this means focusing on what you can influence rather than obsessing over outcomes you can't control.

## Learn From Every Game

After a loss, a good player reviews the game to find where things went wrong. That habit of honest reflection turns setbacks into growth.

## The Bottom Line

Chess doesn't give you answers, but it trains you to think clearly when the stakes are high. The next time pressure mounts, remember the board.

## What Is Geothermal Energy?

Have you ever wondered where the heat in your home comes from? For most of us, it's natural gas, electricity, or oil. But there's another source of heat that's always there, deep beneath our feet: the Earth itself. Geothermal energy comes from the Greek words *geo*, meaning "earth," and *therme*, meaning "heat." It's the heat stored inside the planet, and it's been there since the Earth formed billions of years ago.

## Where Does the Heat Come From?

The Earth is not a solid ball of rock. It has layers, and the center is incredibly hot, possibly hotter than the surface of the Sun. This heat comes from two main sources. First, leftover heat from when the Earth was formed. Second, heat from radioactive elements like uranium and thorium that slowly break down deep underground. This heat slowly moves outward, and it's what keeps the inside of the Earth warm.

## How Do We Use It?

Geothermal energy can be used in two main ways. The first is for electricity. In places like Iceland, New Zealand, and parts of California, hot water or steam from underground is brought to the surface and used to turn turbines, which generate power. The second way is direct use. Hot water from the ground can heat homes, greenhouses, and even swimming pools. It can also be used for bathing and farming.

## Why Is It Special?

Geothermal energy is a renewable resource because the Earth's heat is constantly being replenished. It also produces very little pollution compared to burning coal or oil. It works day and night, rain or shine, so it's a reliable source of power. However, it's not available everywhere, since you need hot ground close to the surface.

## Why Should You Care?

As the world looks for cleaner ways to power our lives, geothermal energy is one of the tools scientists and engineers are using. Maybe one day you'll help find new ways to tap into the Earth's hidden heat.

Have you ever wondered what happens when you stop running and start walking?

## The Day I Stopped Running

In 2019, I was fifty years old and had just been laid off. I had spent thirty years climbing the ladder, and suddenly there was no ladder. I felt like a stranger in my own life. My friends were busy with kids and mortgages, and I was sitting at home, staring at the ceiling. I needed something to do, and I needed something to prove to myself that I could still do it.

So I signed up for the Camino de Santiago, the pilgrimage route from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port to Santiago de Compostela. I had never hiked more than a few miles in my life.

## What the Walk Taught Me

The first week was brutal. My feet blistered, my knees ached, and I cried on the side of the road more than once. But something strange happened. Every morning, I woke up with no plan and no pressure. I just had to put one foot in front of the other.

I learned to slow down. I learned to talk to strangers, to share bread with pilgrims from all over the world, and to listen to the silence between the footsteps. I learned that a long day is not a failure, and that rest is part of the journey, not a break from it.

## Who I Became

When I finally reached the cathedral in Santiago, I didn't feel triumphant. I felt small, and I felt whole. I came home with aching feet and a lighter heart.

I started walking again, this time for joy. I took up gardening, I started volunteering at the library, and I finally began to enjoy the mornings. I discovered that I was not defined by my job or my age. I was a person who could keep going, even when the road was long.

So if you're feeling lost, or stuck, or like you've lost your way, maybe the answer isn't to run faster. Maybe it's to take a step, and then another, and trust that the path will show up.

Thank you.

WIND OVER THE WATERS: BUILDING AND IMPACTS OF OFFSHORE WIND FARMS

Offshore wind farms are among the fastest-growing sources of clean energy. They harness steady winds over the sea, where turbines can generate far more power than on land. Building one is a massive engineering effort, and its effects on marine life are complex.

**How They're Built**

Construction begins with site surveys, including seabed mapping, weather data, and environmental assessments. Once a location is approved, vessels install foundations, often steel jackets, monopiles, or floating platforms, depending on water depth.

Turbines are then lifted into place by specialized cranes. Cables carry electricity to shore, where it joins the grid. A single farm may contain dozens of turbines, plus substations, mooring systems, and sometimes artificial reefs.

**Impacts on Marine Ecosystems**

The effects vary by species and location.

*Positive effects:* Foundations can become artificial reefs, attracting fish, crustaceans, and invertebrates. Some studies show increased biodiversity around turbine bases.

*Negative effects:* Construction disturbs seabed sediment, which can harm benthic organisms. Noise from pile-driving can stress marine mammals, though quieter techniques like bubble curtains help.

*Habitat changes:* Turbines and cables can alter local currents and light levels.

*Wildlife interactions:* Birds and bats may collide with blades, and some marine mammals may avoid certain areas.

**Balancing Growth and Conservation**

Careful planning, seasonal construction, and ongoing monitoring can reduce harm. Many farms now include environmental offsets and long-term research.

Offshore wind offers a promising path toward cleaner energy. With thoughtful management, it can coexist with healthy ocean ecosystems.

and if you lose to someone with a higher rating, you lose points.
Over many games, your rating settles near the level of the players
you regularly beat.

HOW THE NUMBERS WORK

Ratings are usually grouped into broad ranges:

- 0 to 1000: complete beginner
- 1000 to 1200: learning the basics
- 1200 to 1400: solid beginner
- 1400 to 1600: intermediate
- 1600 to 1800: strong club player
- 1800 to 2000: advanced club player
- 2000+: strong player

These ranges are rough guides. A 1300 player can still beat a
1500 player, and a 1100 player can lose to a 1000 player. Ratings
are not a guarantee of who will win any single game.

WHAT YOUR FIRST RATING MEANS

When you sign up, your rating is often set at 1000 or 1200, or
calculated from your first few games. This is a starting point, not
a final judgment. Your first 10 to 20 games will move your rating
a lot, because the system is still learning how you play.

HOW GAMES CHANGE YOUR RATING

- Winning against a higher-rated player gives you more points.
- Winning against a lower-rated player gives you fewer points.
- Losing to a higher-rated player costs you fewer points.
- Losing to a lower-rated player costs you more points.

A typical game might change your rating by 10 to 20 points.
Stronger players change theirs by more.

TIPS FOR A NEWCOMER

1. Don't panic over early losses. Everyone starts somewhere.
2. Play rated games only when you are relaxed and focused.
3. Review your games to learn from mistakes.
4. Expect your rating to rise slowly as you improve.
5. Remember that the goal is to enjoy the game, not just climb.

Trekking poles are adjustable walking sticks that hikers use to support their weight and improve balance. Most modern poles are made of aluminum or carbon fiber and can be collapsed into a compact length for transport. At the top, a basket of plastic or rubber cups sits around the tip. These baskets spread the load over a wider area of the ground, which prevents the pole from sinking into soft soil, mud, or snow. The tip itself is usually a carbide point that grips firm ground and resists slipping. Many poles also have a wrist strap, so you can hang your weight on the pole without gripping it tightly. Some models include a shock absorber, a spring mechanism that cushions the impact when you plant the pole.

The main benefit of poles is that they share the load between your legs and your arms. When you step down, your body absorbs the force through your knees, hips, and ankles. Poles transfer a portion of that force to your upper body, which can reduce strain on your joints. This is especially helpful on long descents, where downhill walking puts heavy pressure on the knees. Poles also give you something to push against when climbing, which can make steep sections feel easier. On uneven terrain, poles act as extra points of contact, helping you spot rocks, roots, and loose ground before your feet reach them. They can also improve your rhythm and cadence, since a steady pole swing can encourage a more efficient stride.

For a beginner, the question is whether these advantages outweigh the extra weight and effort. The honest answer is that poles are not essential, but they can be a smart investment if you plan to hike often or in challenging conditions. If you only take short, flat walks on well-maintained trails, you may never notice a difference. In that case, carrying poles adds a few ounces to your pack and requires a small adjustment to your gait.

There are also practical reasons to consider poles. They can double as a tent stake, a tool for clearing snow, or a way to test the depth of a stream. They are also useful for people with knee problems, older hikers, or anyone recovering from an injury. Beginners who are unsure can rent poles at many trailheads and outdoor shops, which lets them try them before buying.

Ultimately, the decision depends on your goals and comfort level. If you want to build confidence, protect your knees, and enjoy longer hikes, poles are worth it. If you are just starting out and want to keep things simple, you can skip them and add them later.

Margaret Hale had run her flower shop for eleven years, and she had never once sent a marketing email to her entire customer list. She had never even wanted to.

But on a Tuesday in March, her laptop froze, and she hit "send" before she could think.

The subject line read: *URGENT: Your Bouquet is Waiting (and we are very sorry for the typo)*.

The body was worse. It began, "Dear valued customer, we are very sorry for the typo in your bouquet. We have made a mistake and we are very sorry."

Margaret stared at the screen. She had meant to say "typo in your order." Instead, she had written "typo in your bouquet."

She should have deleted it. She should have called her ISP. She should have cried.

Instead, she laughed until her ribs ached.

By Thursday, the shop was crowded. A man holding a single red rose asked if he could buy the whole display. A teenager wanted a bouquet that said "I'm sorry" in giant letters. A grandmother asked for a dozen roses with a note that read, "I'm sorry I forgot your birthday."

Margaret had never sold more than forty bouquets in a week. She sold three hundred and twelve.

The next morning, she sent a follow-up email. It was short. It said: "We are very sorry for the typo. Thank you for the flowers."

She did not mention the sales.

**Tips for Hiking in the Rain and Staying Dry and Comfortable**

1. **Dress in layers, not in cotton.** Cotton soaks up water, holds it against your skin, and takes forever to dry, which can lead to chilling. Choose a moisture-wicking base layer, an insulating mid-layer like fleece or down, and a waterproof, breathable outer shell.

2. **Invest in a good rain jacket and pants.** Look for a jacket with a waterproof rating of at least 10,000 mm and sealed seams. A hood that fits over your helmet or hat is a useful bonus.

3. **Wear waterproof boots with good traction.** Wet rocks and mud become slippery, so grippy soles matter. Waterproof boots keep your feet drier, and dry feet are the single biggest factor in staying comfortable.

4. **Pack a lightweight pack cover or plastic bag.** A simple trash bag over your pack keeps your gear dry, and a dedicated pack cover is worth the small investment.

5. **Bring a spare set of clothes.** Pack a dry shirt, socks, and underwear in a sealed bag. Changing into dry layers when you get soaked is far more comfortable than staying wet.

6. **Use gaiters.** These keep mud, water, and debris out of your boots, which is especially helpful on wet, muddy trails.

7. **Carry a headlamp.** Rainy days often bring shorter daylight hours, and visibility drops quickly in overcast or stormy conditions.

8. **Bring a small towel or microfiber cloth.** Wiping your face, hands, and neck helps you stay comfortable, and drying off after a swim or crossing a stream is a nice perk.

9. **Pack snacks and extra calories.** Cold, wet conditions burn more energy, so eat regularly to keep your body warm.

10. **Bring a first-aid kit and blister care.** Wet feet rub more easily, so carry moleskin or blister pads.

11. **Check the forecast and trail conditions.** Look at weather apps and recent trail reports before you go.

12. **Know when to turn back.** If the rain turns into a storm, visibility drops, or the trail becomes dangerous, head back. No hike is worth risking your safety.

13. **Stay hydrated.** Rainy weather can be deceptively hot, so drink water even if you don't feel thirsty.

14. **Keep your hands warm.** Gloves or mittens are easy to forget but make a big difference in comfort.

15. **Plan for a dry place to rest.** If you have to stop, find a sheltered spot like a rock overhang or a tree, and sit on something dry.

The short version: your unique selling proposition (USP) is the one thing customers choose you for over every other food truck in the area.

compass points for our club's debate on trail permits

**Arguments for permits and quotas**

- **Crowd control:** Fixed daily limits spread hikers across the day, so no single section is packed at dawn.
- **Wildlife protection:** Fewer people mean less disturbance to nesting birds, elk, and other sensitive species.
- **Trail preservation:** Quotas reduce erosion, trampling of vegetation, and damage to fragile alpine or desert ecosystems.
- **Safety:** Thinner crowds make it easier for rescuers to locate and reach hikers in trouble.
- **Fair access:** A lottery or reservation system can give local residents and long-time members priority over casual visitors.
- **Funding:** Permit fees often go directly into trail maintenance and ranger staffing.

**Arguments against permits and quotas**

- **Cost:** Fees can be steep, and some argue they price out families, students, and low-income hikers.
- **Bureaucracy:** Online applications, waitlists, and strict rules can frustrate people who simply want to hike.
- **Inequity:** Systems that favor those with reliable internet or flexible schedules may disadvantage rural residents.
- **Reduced spontaneity:** The joy of a last-minute trip to the trailhead disappears.
- **Enforcement challenges:** Rangers may struggle to monitor compliance, and some hikers may simply ignore the rules.
- **Diminishing returns:** Critics argue that a few extra hikers rarely cause lasting harm, and that education and stewardship matter more.

**What our club might consider**

- Supporting a modest, transparent fee structure
- Advocating for local priority in reservation systems
- Promoting Leave No Trace practices on every outing

# Islands Rising from the Deep: How Underwater Volcanoes Build New Land

Beneath the ocean's surface, a quiet revolution is constantly underway. Every year, underwater volcanoes erupt and slowly push up fresh rock, and over centuries these eruptions can give birth to entirely new islands.

It all begins with plate tectonics. Where tectonic plates pull apart, such as along the Mid-Ocean Ridge, magma rises to fill the gap. This creates a long chain of submarine volcanoes, many of which never break the surface. When a volcano does grow tall enough to pierce the water, it becomes an island. Iceland is the most famous example, sitting right on the ridge.

The process is gradual. A single eruption may add only a few meters of rock, but repeated eruptions over thousands of years can build a mountain hundreds of meters high. Once the island emerges, waves and wind begin to shape it, and plants and animals start to colonize the new land.

Some underwater volcanoes are far more dramatic. In 2018, the Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcano erupted with such force that it sent a pressure wave circling the globe. Scientists are still studying how such events affect the ocean and atmosphere.

For ocean science enthusiasts, these volcanoes offer a living laboratory. They reveal how Earth's interior connects to its surface, how life adapts to extreme conditions, and how landscapes are never truly finished. The next island you see may have been born just a few centuries ago, still rising from the deep.

**Review: A Weekend Farmers Market Booth for a Small-Batch Hot Sauce Maker**

For a maker producing a few dozen bottles a week, the farmers market is one of the most effective marketing channels available. It turns an abstract product into something people can see, smell, and taste.

**Strengths**

The biggest advantage is direct feedback. Watching customers sample a chipotle habanero blend and ask whether it's "too hot" tells you more about flavor preferences than any survey. You can also spot which sauces sell fastest and adjust your lineup accordingly.

Face time builds loyalty. A friendly conversation about where the peppers come from or how the sauce is aged creates a personal connection that online ads can't match. Many customers return because they remember the person behind the bottle.

The booth also serves as a live storefront. A well-styled table with fresh peppers, tasting cups, and a handwritten sign about your process draws attention and makes the brand feel authentic.

**Weaknesses**

Costs add up quickly. Booth fees, parking, and supplies can eat into thin margins, especially if sales are slow on a given weekend. Weather is another risk, since rain can cancel a day of sales entirely.

Competition is fierce. Shoppers may walk past your table if it's crowded or poorly positioned. You also miss out on customers who aren't market-goers, so the market alone won't build a broad following.

**Tips for Success**

- Offer a small free sample to encourage first-time buyers.
- Collect email addresses for a newsletter or loyalty program.
- Share booth photos on social media to reach people who couldn't attend.
- Keep inventory light to avoid waste.

**Verdict**

The farmers market is a strong starting point for building a local following, provided you treat it as part of a larger strategy rather than your only channel.

Have you ever wondered how something as simple as watching birds could make a difference in your daily life?

## A Gentle Way to Stay Active

Bird watching is one of the most accessible forms of outdoor activity available to us. It requires no special equipment beyond a pair of binoculars, a comfortable chair, and a willingness to look up. A short walk around the garden, a visit to the pond, or a stroll along the nature trail can keep your legs moving and your mind alert. Many birders also keep journals, sketch feathers, or learn to identify calls, which adds a satisfying mental challenge. These small efforts add up: regular movement supports heart health, balance, and mood, while the quiet focus of listening for a robin or a woodpecker can ease stress and sharpen attention.

## Building Community Through Shared Interest

Perhaps the greatest gift of bird watching is the connection it creates. Joining a local birding club, attending a community walk, or sharing sightings with neighbors gives you a reason to step outside your home and meet others. These gatherings often include people of all ages, offering natural opportunities for conversation, friendship, and a sense of belonging. Even a simple group outing to spot a rare warbler can become a cherished memory. For those who prefer to stay at home, phone calls, video chats, and shared photo albums keep the hobby lively and the friendships strong.

P.P.S. Consider joining a local birding group or starting a small club at your community center. Your next sighting could be the beginning of a new friendship.

FINDING CALM IN THE WILDS

Many people today feel a heavy weight on their shoulders. Work, bills, and worries can crowd the mind until it feels hard to breathe. Bird watching offers a quiet way to step back from that noise.

When you sit still to watch a bird, you must pay close attention. You notice the shape of a wing, the flash of a red breast, or the soft call of a sparrow. These small details pull your mind away from the past and the future, where much of our stress lives. You are here, now, in the moment.

Birds also move with a calm, steady rhythm. A robin hops from branch to branch, and a hawk glides on the wind. Watching them can help you slow your own pace and find a sense of peace.

Another gift of bird watching is that it is free and open to all. You need no special gear, only a pair of eyes and a quiet spot. A park bench, a garden, or a forest trail can become a place of rest.

Finally, birds remind us that life goes on, no matter what we feel. A flock may fly past, and the world keeps turning. This simple truth can ease the fear that our worries will never end.

So the next time you feel overwhelmed, step outside and look up. The birds are waiting, and so is your calm.

Did you ever argue over a ceiling fan?

The ladder's wobbly, the box is heavy,
and you're already shouting at me
about the level, about the screws,
about the way I hold the blade.

"You're leaning on the wrong side!"
"I'm leaning on the right side!"
The drywall whispers, "Please, just stop."

We've argued over dinner, over bills,
over whose turn it is to take the trash,
but never over a fan.
This is new. This is strange.

I reach for the bracket, you reach for the cord,
our hands brush, and we both freeze.
The room is silent except for the hum
of the old fan still spinning above us.

Then you say, "I'm sorry," and I say, "Me too,"
and we both laugh at how ridiculous
we sound, two grown people
arguing about a ceiling.

We start again. You hold the bracket,
I hold the cord, and we don't let go.
We measure twice, we measure again,
and this time we agree.

The fan turns slowly, gently,
like a slow apology,
and the room feels lighter,
like we've finally found our balance.

**Marketing and advertising are not the same thing, but advertising is a part of marketing.** Think of marketing as the entire plan for reaching and serving customers, and advertising as one tool you use within that plan.

**Marketing is the big picture.** It starts with understanding who your customers are, what they need, and how they make decisions. For example, if you run [business name], you might discover that your ideal customer is a busy parent who values convenience and trusts local recommendations. Marketing covers everything you do to attract, keep, and grow those customers. That includes:

- **Product:** What you sell and how it solves a problem.
- **Price:** How much you charge and why.
- **Place:** Where customers can buy, such as [website URL] or [physical address].
- **Promotion:** All the ways you communicate, including advertising, social media, email, and public relations.
- **Customer experience:** How people feel before, during, and after buying.

**Advertising is a paid form of promotion.** It is a message you pay to show to a specific audience. A billboard, a Facebook ad, a radio spot, or a sponsored post are all advertising. Advertising helps you reach people quickly, but it does not, by itself, build a lasting relationship with them.

**A simple way to remember the difference:** Marketing is the strategy, and advertising is one tactic. You could have excellent marketing with no advertising at all, such as a bakery that relies on word of mouth and a loyal neighborhood following. Conversely, you could spend heavily on advertising with poor marketing, such as promoting a product nobody wants, and still see little return.

**Why this matters for you.** Before you spend money on ads, ask: Who am I selling to? What makes my offering different? Where do my customers already spend time? Answering these questions first makes your advertising more effective and your budget more efficient.

**A practical example.** Suppose you sell handmade candles at [store name]. Your marketing might include a website, a loyalty program, and partnerships with local boutiques. Your advertising might be a $500 Facebook campaign targeting people within 10 miles of [city name]. The campaign supports the broader plan, but it is not the whole plan.

**Your next step.** Start by writing a short marketing plan that defines your target customer, your unique value, and your main channels. Then decide which advertising channels fit that plan. Test small, measure results, and adjust. Over time, you'll see how each piece works together to grow your business.

Setting up a backyard feeding station that welcomes songbirds while discouraging squirrels takes a little planning, but the results are worth it. Follow these steps to create a welcoming habitat.

First, choose a location. Place feeders near trees or shrubs where birds can land and take cover, but keep them at least ten feet away from the house. This distance makes it harder for squirrels to reach the food.

Next, select the right feeders. Tube feeders with small perches and weight-sensitive ports are excellent choices. When a squirrel lands, the feeder closes automatically. Suet cages and nectar feeders also appeal to many species.

Then, offer a variety of food. Black oil sunflower seeds attract finches and chickadees, while nyjer draws goldfinches. Suet is rich in fat and favored by woodpeckers and wrens. Avoid bread and stale crumbs, which can spoil quickly.

To keep squirrels away, use baffles. A dome or cone-shaped guard mounted above the feeder stops climbing. You can also hang feeders from bungee cords or chains, which sway and make it difficult for squirrels to balance.

Finally, maintain the station regularly. Clean feeders every two weeks with a mild bleach solution to prevent disease. Refill food as needed and remove it during hot weather.

With patience and care, your yard can become a thriving haven. "A well-placed feeder can turn a quiet corner into a lively gathering place." Over time, you may find yourself enjoying "a wealth of visitors, from sparrows to hummingbirds."

engine of any serious birder's library, the Sibley Guide to Birds has quietly become the standard for many of us, and it deserves a closer look from our older members who grew up with the older classics.

The most striking difference is the size. Sibley is a hefty volume, and its plates are large, detailed, and painted with a painterly quality that makes each species feel alive. Older guides such as the National Geographic Field Guide and the Peterson series were smaller, more portable, and often relied on line drawings or simplified color plates. Sibley's artistry is a real strength, but it comes at a cost in weight and price.

Identification is where the gap is widest. Sibley includes range maps, seasonal notes, and a wealth of behavioral detail that the older guides rarely offered. Its range maps are especially useful for spotting vagrants and planning trips. The older guides were built for quick, on-the-ground identification, and they still excel at that. Their compact format and clear, practical keys make them far easier to carry on a long walk.

The older guides also have a charm that Sibley lacks. Sibley's paintings are beautiful, yet they can be harder to match to a bird in the field, especially in poor light or at a distance.

**Mount Rainier Lahar Warning Siren: What to Do**

Mount Rainier is one of the most active volcanoes in the Cascade Range. Lahars are fast-moving flows of water, mud, rock, and debris that can travel down river valleys at speeds exceeding 30 miles per hour. They can destroy homes, roads, and bridges within minutes. If you live near the mountain, you must know how to respond.

**1. Know Your Siren**
The warning siren is loud, continuous, and unmistakable. It may sound like a deep, sustained wail. If you hear it, treat it as an emergency. Do not wait to confirm the cause.

**2. Act Immediately**
When the siren sounds, leave your home right away. Do not gather belongings, pack a bag, or wait for family members. Lahars can arrive faster than you can drive. Your life is more important than your possessions.

**3. Go Up, Not Down**
Move to the highest ground available. Lahars flow downhill, so elevation is your best protection. If you are in a valley, head toward the ridge or a hillside. Avoid riverbeds, canyons, and low-lying areas.

**4. Leave the Valley**
If you are in a valley and cannot reach high ground, leave the valley entirely. Drive to the nearest town or open area away from the river. Do not stop to check on your home or to wait for others.

**5. Stay Away from Waterways**
Do not cross rivers, streams, or bridges during a warning. Lahars can surge through them and wash out crossings.

**6. Follow Official Guidance**
Listen for updates from the National Weather Service, Washington State Department of Natural Resources, or local emergency management. Follow evacuation orders and road closures.

**7. After the Siren Stops**
Do not return home until officials say it is safe. Lahars can continue for hours, and debris may remain unstable.

**8. Prepare Ahead of Time**
- Learn the evacuation routes for your area.
- Keep a go-bag with essentials.
- Know the location of the nearest high ground.
- Share your plan with family and neighbors.

**Remember:** A siren means danger is possible. Your fastest, safest choice is to get to high ground immediately.

Before the fifteenth century, most books in Europe were copied by hand, and the process was slow, expensive, and prone to error. A single scribe might spend months producing one volume, and the result was often riddled with mistakes. Because of these costs, books were rare treasures owned mainly by churches, monasteries, and wealthy nobles. Ordinary people rarely saw a printed page, and ideas traveled slowly from one scholar to another through letters, lectures, and occasional manuscripts.

Johannes Gutenberg changed this situation around 1450 with his movable type printing press. His invention combined several earlier ideas into a practical system. He used metal letters that could be arranged into lines, inked, and pressed onto paper. He also developed an oil-based ink that worked well on metal type and a press adapted from wine presses. These innovations made it possible to produce many identical copies quickly and at a fraction of the cost of hand copying.

The first major work printed in Europe was the Gutenberg Bible, completed around 1455. Its quality astonished readers, and it showed that books could be made both beautiful and affordable. Within a few decades, printing shops appeared in cities across the continent, including Mainz, Strasbourg, Paris, Venice, and later London. By the end of the century, thousands of titles had been printed, covering theology, science, law, history, and literature.

This rapid growth of printed material transformed how knowledge spread. Ideas no longer depended on a single scholar's memory or a monastery's library. A new book could reach hundreds of readers almost immediately, and printers often corrected errors in later editions. Scholars could compare texts more easily, which helped standardize languages and improve accuracy in fields like medicine and astronomy.

The press also changed who could access learning. As books became cheaper, students, merchants, and even some women began to own them. Literacy gradually increased, and reading became a skill worth teaching. Religious ideas spread especially quickly, since pamphlets and Bibles could be distributed widely and cheaply.

Perhaps the most important effect was that knowledge became a shared public resource rather than a private possession. Ideas could be challenged, debated, and improved by many people at once. This openness laid the groundwork for the Renaissance, the Reformation, and eventually the Scientific Revolution.

In short, Gutenberg's press turned knowledge from something few could own into something many could share. It reshaped European society and set the stage for the modern world.

Why do so many people compare the printing press to the internet?

Both technologies dramatically lowered the cost of reproducing information. Before printing, copying texts required scribes and took enormous effort. After printing, books could be produced quickly and sold cheaply. The internet repeats this pattern by making digital content nearly free to share.

Both also broke the monopoly that institutions once held over knowledge. Monasteries, universities, and governments previously controlled what people could read. Printing allowed pamphlets, newspapers, and books to reach ordinary readers. The internet extends this by letting anyone publish a blog or video.

Both reshaped how ideas spread across society and geography. Ideas no longer traveled slowly through personal networks or oral tradition. Instead, they could reach thousands of people almost instantly. This speed helped spread scientific discoveries, religious reform, and political movements.

Both changed the relationship between readers and the written word. People began to consume information more actively rather than passively. Literacy and critical thinking became more important for everyday life.

However, the comparison has important limits worth remembering. The printing press was a one-way, relatively slow technology. The internet is interactive, allowing instant feedback and conversation. It also enables misinformation to spread far more quickly than ever.

Ultimately, both technologies show how tools shape the flow of ideas. Each one reshaped culture, politics, and the way humans learn.

High performers are often admired for their relentless drive, their ability to deliver under pressure, and their habit of working through long hours. The result is a dangerous cycle. The more they push, the more they need to push to feel productive, until the cost of stopping feels greater than the cost of continuing.

Breaking the cycle starts with recognizing that rest is not a reward for finishing work. It is a necessary part of doing good work. High performers should treat boundaries as a professional skill, not a weakness.

**The Quiet Case for Decaf**

Decaf coffee has long carried a reputation for being dull, bitter, and somehow less real than its caffeinated cousin. That prejudice is mostly a myth, and it deserves a closer look.

The problem is that most people judge decaf by the cheapest version they have ever tasted. Cheap decaf is often over-roasted to mask the subtle flavors that remain after the caffeine is removed, and it is brewed with water that is too hot or too cold. The result is a flat, burnt-tasting brew that confirms the stereotype.

Better decaf tells a different story. Specialty roasters now use methods such as Swiss water processing, which extracts caffeine without harsh chemicals, and they roast their beans with the same care they give caffeinated lots. A well-made decaf can be bright, fruity, and complex, with notes of chocolate, stone fruit, or caramel that rival any espresso.

The numbers back this up. In 2024, a survey of 7818 coffee drinkers found that nearly half of them had upgraded to specialty decaf within the past year, and many said the switch changed how they thought about coffee altogether.

There is also a practical side to consider. Decaf lets people enjoy the ritual of coffee without the jitters, the late-night insomnia, or the afternoon crash. For many, it is simply a more thoughtful way to drink.

So the next time you reach for a cup, ask whether you are judging decaf by its reputation or by its quality. The answer may surprise you.

# The Coffee Ceremony: Ethiopia's Living Tradition

Ethiopia is the birthplace of coffee. The plant likely grew wild in the highlands long ago. Today, coffee remains deeply woven into daily life.

The coffee ceremony is a ritual that can last hours. It usually begins with washing the roasting pan. Next, green beans are roasted over an open fire. The aroma fills the room as the beans turn dark.

Roasted beans are then ground by hand. A traditional mortar and pestle makes a coarse, fragrant paste. The paste is brewed in a clay pot called a jebena.

The host pours the coffee into small cups. Guests drink it slowly, often three rounds. Each round is called a different name. The first is called abol, the second tona, and the third baraka.

This ceremony is more than a way to drink coffee. It is a time for conversation and connection. Elders share stories while younger people listen. Neighbors gather to catch up and build trust.

The ceremony also marks important life events. Weddings, births, and funerals often include it. It welcomes visitors and honors guests alike.

In a fast-changing world, the ceremony endures. It reminds people to slow down and connect.

**Arabica vs. Robusta: A Beginner's Guide**

When you buy coffee, the first thing to notice is the bean. There are TWO main species: Arabica and Robusta. They taste VERY different, and knowing the difference helps you choose what you like.

**Arabica** is the favorite of specialty coffee lovers. It grows at HIGH altitudes, often above 1,200 meters, in cool, mountainous regions like Ethiopia, Colombia, and Brazil. Because it grows slowly, Arabica beans are SMOOTHER, SWEETER, and more complex. You might taste notes of chocolate, fruit, berries, or caramel. Arabica also has a lower caffeine content, about 1.2 to 1.4 percent.

**Robusta** is hardier. It grows at lower altitudes, tolerates heat and pests better, and produces MORE beans per plant. That makes it CHEAPER. Robusta has a STRONGER, BITTERER flavor, often described as woody, nutty, or even rubbery. It contains roughly TWICE the caffeine of Arabica, which is why it is popular in espresso blends and instant coffee.

**Why it matters**

Most specialty coffee is 100 percent Arabica. Blends with Robusta are common in everyday coffee shops because Robusta adds body and a bold kick. If you want a delicate, nuanced cup, look for SINGLE ORIGIN Arabica. If you love a punchy, intense espresso, a blend with Robusta may suit you.

**Taste test tip**

Brew a cup of each and compare. Notice the sweetness, the acidity, and the aftertaste. Your preference is PERSONAL, and there is NO WRONG answer.

village life often depends on the weather, and forecasters use two big ideas to explain it: high and low pressure systems.

**High pressure** means the air is sinking. As it falls, it warms and dries out, so clouds can't form easily. This usually brings clear skies, sunshine, and calm winds.

**Low pressure** means the air is rising. Rising air cools, and the moisture inside it condenses into clouds and rain. Low pressure often brings storms, wind, and sometimes snow.

Forecasters look at maps showing where these systems are and how they move. They also check satellite images, radar, and data from weather stations. A national weather agency combines all this information to make predictions.

Think of it like driving on a road: you can't see the whole route at once, but by watching the signs ahead, you can guess what's coming. Forecasters do the same with weather.

So, if a high pressure system is moving toward you, expect sunny days. If a low pressure system is approaching, prepare for storms.

before the 1960s, weather forecasting relied almost entirely on ground stations, ships, and balloons. forecasters pieced together a patchwork of observations, and large areas of the ocean and atmosphere remained invisible. the launch of the first weather satellites, including the united states' tiros-1 in 1960 and the european meteorological agency's meteor-1 in 1965, changed that. for the first time, scientists could see clouds, storms, and temperature patterns across entire continents and oceans.

the early satellites were limited. they were slow, their images were grainy, and they captured only a few snapshots each day. still, they gave forecasters a new perspective. by the 1970s, polar-orbiting satellites provided daily global coverage, and geostationary satellites began watching the same spot continuously. these tools helped track hurricanes, predict rainfall, and study climate patterns.

the next leap came with satellites that could "see" beyond visible light. infrared sensors measured heat, revealing cloud tops and temperature changes even at night. microwave sensors could peer through clouds to detect rain and snow. these advances made forecasts more accurate and allowed scientists to study the atmosphere in three dimensions.

today, satellites work alongside radar, weather balloons, aircraft, and ocean buoys. supercomputers combine all of this data into numerical models that simulate how the atmosphere will evolve. forecasters now issue predictions days ahead with far greater confidence, and they can warn people about severe storms hours earlier than before.

the story of weather forecasting is a story of technology. from scattered observations to a global, connected view of the sky, satellites have turned weather prediction into one of the most useful and life-saving sciences we have.

<<Reading Your Coffee Bag Like a Pro>>

That little bag of beans you bought at the café is packed with clues. Here's what the most common terms on a specialty coffee bag actually mean.

**Washed (or Washed Process)**

Washed coffee is the most common style. The fruit is removed from the cherry, and the beans are fermented in water to strip away the remaining pulp. The result is a clean, bright cup with clear acidity and defined flavors. Think citrus, tea, or floral notes.

**Natural (or Natural Process)**

Natural coffee is dried with the fruit still attached. The beans absorb sugars and compounds from the cherry, which gives a heavier body, sweeter fruitiness, and sometimes funky or winey notes. It's the riskier method, and a bad natural can taste sour or fermented.

**Honey Process**

A middle ground between washed and natural. Some of the fruit is left on the bean during drying, giving a cup with more body and sweetness than washed but less intensity than natural.

**Single Origin**

This means the coffee comes from one farm, one region, or one country. It's like a varietal wine: you can trace the flavor back to a specific place. Single origins often highlight terroir, the way soil, climate, and elevation shape the taste.

**Blend**

A mix of beans from different origins, chosen to create a consistent flavor profile. Blends are often designed for balance and reliability rather than showcasing a single place.

**Altitude**

Altitude is the height above sea level where the coffee was grown. Higher elevations mean cooler temperatures, which slow the bean's development. The result is denser beans with more complex, nuanced flavors. Look for numbers like 1,800 meters or 6,000 feet.

**Roast Date**

Freshness matters. Specialty coffee is best within a few weeks of roasting. A roast date tells you when the beans were roasted, not when they were picked.

**Tasting Notes**

These are the flavors the roaster detected during cupping. They're a guide, not a promise. Your own palate may find something different.

**The Bottom Line**

Read the bag, and you'll start noticing why one coffee tastes so different from another.

Have you ever wondered how a single person could turn a few pounds of paper into a crisp printed page?

Here are some tips for explaining the 19th-century iron hand press to visitors of all ages:

1. **Start with a simple question.** Ask visitors what they think happens when they press a button on a modern printer. Then show them that this machine does the same thing, only by hand.

2. **Compare it to something familiar.** A hand press works like a giant lever, much like a seesaw or a bottle opener. The long handle gives the operator mechanical advantage, so a small push becomes a strong squeeze.

3. **Demonstrate the lever action.** Invite a volunteer to pull the handle down while you point out the fulcrum (the pivot point) and the long arm. Kids love feeling the force build up.

4. **Explain the platen and the bed.** The flat iron plate (platen) presses down on the paper, while the bed holds the type and paper steady. Show how the platen moves in a straight line, which is why the press is so precise.

5. **Show the type and ink.** Point out the individual metal letters, called type, set in a frame. Explain that ink is rolled onto the raised letters, and the platen presses the ink onto the paper.

6. **Tell a story.** Share how this press was used in local newspapers, pamphlets, or schoolbooks. Visitors connect better with history when they see it in their own community.

7. **Use simple language.** Avoid technical terms like "bed," "platen," and "chase" unless you explain them. Say "the flat plate" instead of "platen."

8. **Encourage hands-on participation.** Let visitors pull the handle themselves, with supervision. Physical involvement helps everyone remember how it works.

9. **Highlight the human effort.** Emphasize that one person could produce hundreds of pages a day, which was remarkable for the time.

10. **Connect it to modern printing.** Mention that this design inspired the rotary presses used in today's newspapers and magazines.

11. **Keep it short and engaging.** Aim for a 2–3 minute explanation, then open the floor for questions.

12. **Use visuals.** Bring a sample of printed material made on a similar press, or show a diagram of the mechanism.

13. **End with a takeaway.** Ask visitors to think about how information was shared in their grandparents' time, and how it has changed.

**Cleaning and Oiling a Decades-Old Chandler & Price Platen Press**

**1. Prepare the workspace.** Move the press to a well-ventilated area, ideally a garage with open doors, or outdoors on a calm day. Wear safety glasses, nitrile gloves, and a respirator rated for mineral spirits and metal dust. Lay down drop cloths and keep a fire extinguisher nearby.

**2. Disconnect power.** Unplug the press and remove the fuse or circuit breaker. Verify the machine is dead with a multimeter before touching any controls.

**3. Remove the platen.** Loosen the platen bolts and lift the platen off the bed. This exposes the bed, the inking mechanism, and the type bars.

**4. Clean the bed and type bars.** Use a stiff brass brush to remove loose dust and rust. For stubborn grime, apply a light coat of mineral spirits and scrub gently. Avoid steel wool, which can scratch the bed. Wipe everything dry with clean rags.

**5. Inspect the inking tunnel.** The tunnel is the channel where ink travels from the ink roller to the type. Check for dried ink, hardened grease, or corrosion. Scrape out blockages with a plastic scraper, then wipe the tunnel clean.

**6. Check the gears and shafts.** Look for cracked teeth, worn bearings, or seized shafts. If a shaft turns stiffly, it may need penetrating oil and patient tapping with a soft mallet.

**7. Apply penetrating oil.** Spray or drip a light penetrating oil on rusted bolts, pivots, and shafts. Let it sit for several hours, then work each part by hand.

**8. Lubricate the moving parts.** Use a light machine oil, such as 3-in-1 oil, on the type bars, the inking mechanism, and the platen bearings. Apply sparingly, since excess oil attracts dust.

**9. Oil the bed.** Use a heavier oil, such as a 20-weight oil, on the bed itself. Run the press through a few cycles to distribute it evenly.

**10. Reassemble.** Replace the platen and tighten the bolts to the manufacturer's torque specifications.

**11. Test the press.** Run it at low speed without type to check for unusual noise or vibration.

**12. Store properly.** If the press will sit again, coat exposed metal with a thin layer of rust inhibitor and cover it with a breathable cloth.

**A final image:** Picture the press resting in a sunlit meadow, its polished steel gleaming after years of neglect.

**The Little Coffee Bean Who Wanted to Shine**

Once upon a time, in a sunny field in South America, there lived a tiny coffee bean named Coco. Coco was small, round, and a little bit shy. Every morning, the sun would wake up and say, "Good morning, Coco!" and Coco would whisper back, "Good morning, Sun!"

Coco had a big dream. He wanted to become the best cup of coffee in the whole world.

One day, Coco met a wise old bean named Baba. "What do you want to be?" asked Baba.

"I want to be the best cup of coffee ever!" said Coco proudly.

Baba smiled. "That's a wonderful dream. But remember, cause and effect are friends. You must do the right things first, and then good things will happen."

Coco thought about that for a long time.

The next morning, Coco worked hard. He rolled around in the warm sun to get strong and healthy. He drank lots of water from the dew on the leaves. He even helped his friends by sharing his sunshine.

"Creative ideas are important too," said Baba. "Think about how you can help others."

So Coco had a creative idea. He would grow tall and strong so that the farmers could pick him easily. He would be sweet and full of flavor so that people would love him.

Months passed. Coco grew bigger and stronger. Then came the harvest! The farmers picked Coco and carried him to a big city.

In the city, Coco was washed, dried, and roasted. He turned from green to a beautiful golden brown. Then he was ground into tiny pieces and poured into a steaming cup.

A little girl named Maya sat down at a table. She took a deep breath and smelled the coffee. "Wow!" she said. "It smells like chocolate and sunshine!"

She took a sip. Her eyes went wide. "This is the best cup of coffee I've ever tasted!"

Coco was so happy. He had become the best cup of coffee in the world!

But Coco didn't forget his friends. He wanted everyone to taste his special flavor. So he asked the barista to pour a little bit of his coffee into a tiny cup for Maya's friends.

Maya shared her coffee with her friends, and they all said it was delicious.

Coco learned that being the best wasn't just about being special. It was about being kind, working hard, and sharing your goodness with others.

And that, my dear friend, is a story about a little coffee bean who made a big difference.

The End.

# The World's Best Cities for Coffee Lovers

Coffee is more than a drink. It's a culture, a ritual, and a reason to travel. Here are the cities where every cup tells a story.

## 1. Melbourne, Australia
Melbourne is the coffee capital of the Southern Hemisphere. Its cafés are known for flat whites, pour-overs, and a relaxed, creative atmosphere. The city's café culture is so strong that it has earned the nickname "the city of coffee."

## 2. Copenhagen, Denmark
Copenhagen is famous for its cozy cafés and its commitment to sustainability. Many shops use organic beans and offer free refills. The city's design-focused cafés make it a favorite for coffee lovers who appreciate both quality and style.

## 3. Istanbul, Turkey
Istanbul blends Eastern and Western traditions in its coffee culture. Try a Turkish coffee, served in a small cup with a thick, frothy layer on top. The city's historic cafés offer a glimpse into centuries of Ottoman history.

## 4. Kyoto, Japan
Kyoto is known for its matcha, a powdered green tea with a rich, earthy flavor. Many cafés serve matcha lattes and desserts, while traditional tea houses offer a peaceful, meditative experience.

## 5. San Francisco, USA
San Francisco is home to some of the best coffee roasters in the world. The city's coffee scene is known for its innovative brewing methods and its focus on local, sustainable sourcing.

## 6. Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
Ethiopia is the birthplace of coffee, and Addis Ababa is the perfect place to experience its history. Visit a traditional coffee ceremony, where coffee is roasted, ground, and brewed in front of you.

## 7. Vienna, Austria
Vienna is known for its elegant cafés, where coffee is served with pastries and cakes. The city's coffee culture is so strong that it has earned the nickname "the city of coffee."

## 8. Hanoi, Vietnam
Hanoi is famous for its egg coffee, a creamy, sweet drink made with egg yolks and condensed milk. The city's coffee culture is also known for its strong, bold flavors and its relaxed, laid-back atmosphere.

## 9. Buenos Aires, Argentina
Buenos Aires is known for its strong, bold coffee and its relaxed, laid-back atmosphere. The city's coffee culture is so strong that it has earned the nickname "the city of coffee."

## 10. Nairobi, Kenya
Nairobi is home to some of the best coffee farms in the world. Visit a local coffee farm to learn about the coffee-growing process and to taste some of the best coffee in the world.

## Conclusion
No matter where you travel, coffee lovers will find a city that suits their taste. Whether you prefer a strong, bold cup or a creamy, sweet drink, there's a city out there that will make you fall in love with coffee.
